findings.scope: Design, Freshness (D-16), and Risks and rollback, "A stale index on the hook path"
findings.text: The spec says a hand edit reaches the hooks after a drain rebuild, and that a tool call or `knowledge rebuild` brings it into the index. The code says otherwise for two cases. First, `fingerprintOf` (repo.ts:856-876) is three folder listings plus the folders' mtimes, and its own comment says "an edit in place changes neither it nor HEAD". So an uncommitted in-place edit never sets a stale mark. `ensureFresh` (index-store.ts:623-631) uses the same comparison, so a tool call misses it as well, and the hooks keep showing the old text with no time bound. Second, when a rebuild does see an uncommitted change, `rebuildRepo` (index-store.ts:493-503) turns the entry into a draft with the problem "changed outside". Such entries are not searchable, so a hand-edited pinned entry vanishes from session start, the prompt and `knowledge_search` until a person adopts it. A reader would expect a hand edit to show up after the next drain. Neither outcome is named, and neither has a `doctor` warning.
findings.reason: Freshness and Risks state both outcomes of a hand edit. One: an edit made in place and not committed changes neither HEAD nor the fingerprint, so the hooks, the drain and the tools keep the committed text until a person runs knowledge rebuild or knowledge adopt; no time is promised. Two: once a rebuild sees an uncommitted change, part 1 indexes the entry as a draft with the problem `changed outside the engine`, so it is not shown at session start, on a prompt or by knowledge_search until the person adopts it; a pinned entry edited by hand therefore disappears from session start until then. The signal is the one part 1's doctor already gives (`changes made outside the engine; run knowledge adopt`), and the spec names it.

findings.scope: Design, What the agent is shown, Prompt (the floor and the probe), and Risks, "The lexical floor's known leak"
findings.text: The precision claim (at most 1 of 28 unrelated prompts injects) was measured by ADR 0020 on an 18-entry probe, against a rule that also read tags. This part reads different fields (no tags or area; context and subject added), writes the probe fresh with 18 entries again, and runs on corpora the spec itself sizes at three repositories of 2,000 entries. Rule 2 (any three distinct non-generic words anywhere, bodies included) gets more likely to fire as the corpus and the bodies grow. bm25 picks the best 10 candidates from 6,000 long entries, so most prompts will find some entry that passes. The perf corpus measures speed only. Nothing measures false injections at the scale the design targets, so the "stays; the probe pins it" mitigation does not cover the real risk: unrelated entries in front of every prompt.
findings.reason: The spec stops claiming the probe's precision for the scale it sizes. Risks says: the floor was measured by ADR 0020 on 18 entries; with thousands of entries rule 2 (three shared non-generic words anywhere in an entry) finds a match for more prompts, and this part does not measure that, since a generated corpus proves nothing about real entries. What bounds the harm: at most two entries inside 480 characters, under an intro that calls them background. What shows it: knowledge_shown keeps the rule that fired for each row, and status prints how many entries were shown in 24 hours, which is why both stay. What answers it: MIN_SHARED, one constant, to be raised with the team's real entries; the ADR records that as the thing to revisit.

findings.scope: Design, Migration 7 (Speed), and Risks, "A rebuild holds the write lock"
findings.text: The rebuild's write transaction has a target of "under 100 ms, the shortest hook busy timeout", which leaves no margin. A hook that waits behind a 99 ms transaction still has to take the lock for `touchSession`. The figure comes from the gate machine (ADR 0020's proofs ran on an M4 Max), and slower user machines will pass 100 ms. The drain runs up to three rebuilds back to back, and tools call `ensureFresh` from the MCP server whenever they like. When the wait runs out, the spec says the hook prints nothing, memory's brief included. The target needs headroom below the timeout, or the spec must say that losing memory's output is the expected cost.
findings.reason: The rebuild's write transaction has a target of under 50 ms at 2,000 entries on the gate machine, half the shortest hook busy timeout, and AC-15 asserts that figure. The drain rebuilds at most three repositories per run, each in its own transaction, never three inside one lock. Risks says plainly what remains: on a slower machine, or behind any other writer, a hook that waits past its busy timeout prints nothing, memory's brief included, which is what a hook does today behind the drain's other writes and compact.
